title: Life cycles of plants and animals: bean, butterfly and frog
summary: Second graders observe a bean plant, a butterfly and a frog and put the stages of each life cycle in order. They discover what all living things share: they are born, grow, reproduce and die. Students keep an observation journal and show what they learned by drawing and labeling one life cycle.
brief: Life cycles of plants and animals for grade 2 science: a two-week unit of ten 40-minute lessons. Students observe and compare the life cycles of a bean plant, a butterfly and a frog, put the stages in order, and notice what all living things share: they are born, grow, reproduce and die. Start a bean-sprouting observation in the first lesson that students record in an observation journal through the unit, use picture cards for sequencing, and read aloud a picture book where it helps. Short check-ins along the way are practice and are not graded. The only graded work is the final drawing-and-labeling assessment of one life cycle, done in the last lesson and scored with a simple rubric: it is 100% of the unit grade.
policies:
Observation journals, check-ins and quizzes are practice and are not graded. The final life cycle drawing is scored with the rubric; a student who is absent draws it on their return.

Spelling does not count toward the score: a name that can be read, such as "krisalis", is accepted. Read any prompt aloud for a student who needs it.

Beans and other materials are for looking at, never for eating. Tell me about any food allergies before the unit begins.

segments.title: Is it alive?
segments.description:
Welcome students in one sentence and say that in this unit they will watch a bean plant, a butterfly and a frog grow.
Show a picture of a puppy and a picture of a rock.
Each student tells a partner which one is alive and gives one reason.
Hear from one pair.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect: the puppy needs food and water and grows; the rock does not need food or water or grow by itself. If students mention moving or sitting still, explain that movement alone does not tell us whether something is living. The only graded work in the unit is the life cycle drawing and labeling assessment (100% of the unit grade), scored with a rubric. Nothing today is graded.

segments.title: What living things do
segments.description:
Show the chart and read each point aloud.
Point to the puppy: it eats, drinks and breathes, it grows, and it will have puppies.
Point to the rock: it does none of these things.
Students tell a partner one thing a living thing needs. Then everyone shows “grow” by crouching low and rising slowly.
segments.teacherNotes: Say “have babies or make seeds” for reproduce. Do not use the word yet. Common mistake: “If it moves, it is alive.” Remind students that a tree does not walk but is alive.

segments.title: Sort the picture cards
segments.description:
Pairs get the Living or nonliving picture cards and a two-column sorting mat.
They place each of the four cards in the living or nonliving column.
For the oak tree and the cloud, the pair says one reason aloud.
The teacher walks around and listens for the words food, water, grow and babies.
segments.teacherNotes:
The cards show four pictures: a puppy, an oak tree, a rock and a cloud.
Expected sort:
puppy: living
oak tree: living (plants are living)
rock: nonliving
cloud: nonliving (changes shape, but does not eat, drink or have babies)

segments.title: Fix Sam’s mistake
segments.description:
Show Sam’s mistake on the screen.
Each student writes or draws on a whiteboard what they would tell Sam.
Partners compare their answers.
Hear two or three, then agree on one class answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Sam is not right. A toy car moves only when pushed or when batteries run it. It does not eat, grow or have baby cars. Praise answers that use “grow” or “eat”. Check-in only; not graded.

segments.title: Is a dry bean seed living?
segments.description:
Hold up a dry lima bean seed and ask if it is living.
Students show thumbs up or thumbs down.
Explain that a seed is alive and resting until it gets water, and that planting it will show us.
Review the rule: beans are for looking at, never for eating.
segments.teacherNotes: Many students will say no because the seed does not move. Correct fact: a seed holds a tiny living plant. Safety: check food allergy information with the office before distributing beans, and have a student with a legume allergy look through the sealed bag instead of handling seeds. Seeds are small, so keep them out of mouths, noses and ears. Students wash hands after handling seeds.

segments.title: Draw and describe my bean seed
segments.description:
Hand out the observation journals. Each student opens to the first page, Observation journal: my dry bean seed.
Students look at one seed through a hand lens and draw what they see.
Then they finish the sentence starters with words for color, feel and shape.
Read the sentence starters aloud for any student who needs it.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected words: hard, smooth, kidney-shaped, cream or pale green, with a small mark on the curved edge. Spelling does not matter if the word can be read. Students need a pencil and crayons. The journal is practice, not graded.

segments.title: Plant the sprouting bags
segments.description:
Each pair gets a zip bag holding a folded damp paper towel.
The pair adds two seeds, one for each partner, and writes both names on the bag.
The teacher seals the bags and places them where they receive indirect light, away from direct sun.
Students say together: “We will look for changes next time.”
segments.teacherNotes: Wet the towels ahead of time so they are damp, not dripping. Nothing will visibly change today. Roots usually show in about three to seven days. Soak extra lima beans the evening before next time so every pair can open one. Keep the bags sealed after planting, and students wash hands afterward.

segments.title: What living things do, and what is next
segments.description:
Each student tells a partner one thing living things do, in one short sentence.
Tell students that next time they will open a soaked bean seed to find the baby plant inside and look for the first changes in the bags.
Students put the journals away and wash their hands.
segments.teacherNotes: Listen for grow, eat, drink, need water, have babies. Then a half-minute thumbs check: “Does moving mean something is alive?” Thumbs down is right. It shows who still thinks moving means alive.

keyIdeas: Living things need food, water and air, and they grow and change.
Nonliving things, such as a rock or a ball, do not eat, drink, grow or have babies.
Moving is not the test for life. A plant stays in one place and is alive, and a toy car moves and is not.
A dry bean seed is alive. It is resting until it gets water.
Scientists observe closely and record what they see by drawing and describing in a journal.

study.overview: Today you learned how scientists tell if something is alive. Living things need food, water and air, and they grow and change. Nonliving things do not. You sorted picture cards, fixed Sam’s mistake, and looked closely at a dry bean seed. Then you planted seeds in sprouting bags. Next time we will look for the first changes.

points.heading: What living things need and do
points.explanation: Living things need food, water and air. They grow and change. They have babies or make seeds. A puppy is a good example. It eats, drinks and breathes. It grows bigger, and one day it can have puppies of its own. A rock does none of these things. It does not eat or drink, it does not grow by itself, and it does not have babies. So a puppy is living and a rock is nonliving.

points.heading: Moving is not the test for life
points.explanation: Some students think that if something moves, it is alive. That is not the test. A toy car rolls across the floor, but only when you push it or batteries run it. It does not eat, grow or have baby cars, so it is nonliving. An oak tree stays in one place, but it needs water, it grows taller, and it makes acorns. So the oak tree is living. A cloud changes shape in the sky, but it does not eat, drink or have babies. It is nonliving too. Ask these questions: does it need food and water, does it grow, and does it have babies or make seeds?

points.heading: A dry bean seed is alive and resting
points.explanation: A dry bean seed does not move, so it looks like a pebble. But a seed holds a tiny living plant. It is resting until it gets water. Then it grows into a plant that makes new seeds, which is how we know it is living. That is why we put two seeds in each sprouting bag with a damp paper towel. The bags sit in light that is not direct sun. Roots usually show in about three to seven days, so nothing will look different today. Next time we will look for the first changes. Remember the safety rules. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. Keep seeds away from your mouth, nose and ears, and wash your hands after you touch them.

points.heading: Scientists look closely and record what they see
points.explanation: A scientist does not just glance at something. A scientist looks closely, draws what is there, and describes it with words. In your journal you used a hand lens to draw your bean seed. Then you wrote a word for its color, a word for how it feels, and a word for its shape. Here is a different example. Suppose you look at a leaf from the playground. You might draw its pointed tip and the lines on it. You might write: green, thin, shaped like a hand. Draw only what you really see. You will use your journal again to record how your seeds change. If a word can be read, it is a good word, even if the spelling is not perfect.

segments.title: What is inside a seed?
segments.description:
Hand out the observation journals again. Students open to the page with their dry bean seed drawing and tell a partner one word for how the seed looked or felt.
Every student then tells the partner one guess: what is inside the seed?
Hear two guesses. Say that today they will open a soaked seed and find out.

segments.title: Meet the three parts of a seed
segments.description:
Hold up a soaked lima bean next to a dry one. Students tell a partner one way the soaked seed is different.
Open a soaked seed under the document camera: peel off the seed coat, split the two halves, and point to the tiny baby plant.
Name each part and have the class repeat it: seed coat, baby plant, food. Explain that the two halves hold food for the baby plant, like a packed lunch.
Students point to each part on the screen picture and say its name to a partner.
segments.teacherNotes: Soaked lima beans were soaked the evening before. The baby plant is a tiny pale curved shape near the small mark, about the size of a grain of rice. Common mistake: calling the whole seed the baby plant. Say that the baby plant is alive and small.
shown: Seed coat: the thin skin outside. Food: the two big halves. Baby plant: the tiny plant between them.
Steps: peel off the seed coat → open the two halves → find the baby plant

segments.title: Open a bean seed and draw it
segments.description:
Each pair gets a tray, a soaked lima bean and a hand lens. One partner peels off the seed coat and the other opens the two halves.
Pairs look through the lens and find the baby plant.
Each student draws the opened seed in the journal and labels three parts: seed coat, baby plant, food.
The teacher walks around and asks each pair to point to the baby plant.
segments.teacherNotes: Have spare soaked seeds for ones that tear. Spelling does not matter if the label can be read, for example seedcoat or bby plant. Read the steps aloud for any student who needs it. Safety: beans are for looking at, never for eating. Keep seeds and pieces out of mouths, noses and ears. A student with a legume allergy watches through a sealed bag or the document camera instead of handling seeds. Everyone washes hands afterward. Collect pieces on the trays and put them in the trash.

segments.title: Fix Mia’s mistake
segments.description:
Show Mia’s statement on the screen and read it aloud.
Each student writes or draws on a whiteboard what they would tell Mia, using the seed they just opened.
Partners compare their answers. Hear two or three, then agree on one class answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Mia is not right. The seed is not empty. The seed coat is the skin on the outside. The baby plant is inside, with food next to it. Praise answers that point to a part of the opened seed. Check-in only; not graded.

segments.title: Look for changes in our sprouting bags
segments.description:
Each pair takes its sealed sprouting bag from the window, out of direct sun, and looks at its two seeds through the bag with a hand lens. The seeds stay inside the bag.
Students compare these seeds with their dry seed drawing from the first journal page.
Each student finishes the sentence starters on the journal page and draws what the seed looks like now. If no change is visible, students record that it looks the same. Pairs put the bags back on the window.
segments.teacherNotes: After about a day, seeds may look bigger or have a seed coat that is starting to split. If they look unchanged, record that observation. Roots usually show in about three to seven days, so “no root yet” is a good record too. Never open these bags. Read the starters aloud for any student who needs it. Wash hands after handling bags.

segments.title: Tell a partner
segments.description:
Each student tells a partner one short sentence that names one seed part and one thing seen in the bag. A seed that looks unchanged is a good answer.
The teacher listens in as pairs talk.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: seed coat, baby plant or food; and an observation such as a bigger seed, a splitting seed coat or a seed that looks the same. Listen for anyone who still says the seed is empty. Check-in only; not graded.

segments.title: Clean up and what is next
segments.description:
Students put journals away, clear the trays and wash their hands.
Say that the bean seed grows into a plant with flowers, and then makes new seeds.
Tell students that next time they will use picture cards and their journal drawings to put the stages of the bean plant in order.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students that the bags stay on the window and that they will look at them again in the coming days. Count the lenses and trays before students leave.

keyIdeas: A bean seed has three parts we can find: the seed coat, the baby plant and the stored food.
The seed coat is a thin skin that covers and protects the seed.
The baby plant is alive and is tucked between the two food halves. The stored food feeds it until it can make its own.
Scientists record changes by comparing what they see now with what they saw before.

study.overview: You opened a soaked bean seed and looked inside with a hand lens. You found three parts: the seed coat, the baby plant and the stored food. You also looked at the seeds in your sprouting bag and wrote down what you saw. This guide helps you remember the parts and how scientists record changes.

points.heading: A bean seed has three parts
points.explanation: When you open a soaked bean seed, you can find three parts. The seed coat is the thin skin on the outside. It covers the seed and keeps it safe. Inside are two big halves that hold stored food. The third part is the baby plant, which is very small. Think of an apple. The skin covers the apple on the outside, just like a seed coat covers a seed. Remember to look for all three parts when you draw and label an opened seed. Beans are only for looking at. Never put them in your mouth.

points.heading: The baby plant is alive and gets food from the seed
points.explanation: The baby plant is a tiny, pale, curved shape. It is about as big as a grain of rice. It is alive, and it sits tucked in between the two food halves. The food is like a packed lunch. It feeds the baby plant until the plant can make its own food. So a seed is not empty. It holds a living baby plant with food right beside it. Try this when you look at an opened seed. Find the two big food halves first. Then look carefully between them for the small baby plant.

points.heading: Scientists record changes by comparing
points.explanation: A scientist looks at something now and compares it with what they saw before. For your bean, you compare the seed in the bag with your dry seed drawing on the first journal page. Suppose your dry seed drawing shows a small, hard seed. Today you might write, “My seed looks bigger.” You can also draw it and add a word like soft. Use the starters in your journal: “Today my seed looks...” and “It is different from my dry seed because...” Sometimes you cannot see a change yet. Then you write that it looks the same. You might also write “no root yet.” That is a true record, and scientists write those down too. Keep the bag closed and put it back on the window. You will look again in the coming days.

study.overview: A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through, one after another. The bean plant has five stages that always come in the same order. In this guide you can practice the words seed, sprout and seedling. You will also see why the bean’s life cycle goes around like a circle, and how your journal drawings show change. Remember that beans are for looking at, never for eating.

points.heading: The bean plant has five stages in a set order
points.explanation: A bean plant grows through five stages: seed, sprout, seedling, grown plant with flowers, and pods holding new seeds. The order never changes. A plant cannot make pods before it has flowers, and it cannot have flowers before it has grown from a seedling. A good way to remember is to tell the story of one bean: it starts as a hard seed, a root comes out, leaves open up, flowers grow, and then the flowers turn into pods full of new beans. Try telling this story to someone at home, counting each stage on your fingers from one to five.

points.heading: Sprout and seedling: root first, leaves next
points.explanation: Two stages are easy to mix up. A sprout begins when a root comes out of the seed coat. A seedling is a small young plant that has its first leaves. So the clue is root first, leaves next. Not every young plant is a sprout, so look for the clues. Here is an example from our sprouting bags. Suppose your seed looks bigger, softer and wrinkly, but you cannot see a root yet. It is still a seed. You can say, “Not a sprout yet.” Good scientists only use the word sprout when they can see the root.

points.heading: The bean life cycle goes around like a circle
points.explanation: The pods hold new seeds, and each new seed can start the cycle again. That is why we draw the stages in a circle with arrows. A circle has no one starting spot, so we choose to begin our picture with a seed. Picture one green pod split open with a row of seeds inside. Each of those seeds can sprout and grow into a new bean plant, which will make flowers and pods of its own. Try drawing the five stages in a circle with arrows to show how the cycle keeps going.

points.heading: Journal drawings show how a living thing changes
points.explanation: Scientists draw in a journal to show how a living thing changes over time. When you draw your bean on different days, you can look back and see what is new. Use your sentence starters: “My bean looks ____. I see ____.” For example, you could write “My bean looks bigger. I see a white root.” Then look at your first drawing and your newest drawing, and use the words seed and sprout to tell which stage each one shows. Spelling does not matter if the word can be read. Always look through the sealed bag, and keep it closed.

segments.title: Four stages of a butterfly

Draw the four stages on the board in a circle with arrows. Explain that the adult butterfly lays new eggs, so the cycle starts again like the bean plant circle.
segments.teacherNotes: Key facts: the caterpillar hatches from the egg and eats leaves; inside the chrysalis it changes; the adult comes out with wings. Common mistake: calling the caterpillar the baby of a worm, or saying the egg holds a butterfly. Say “lays new eggs”, not reproduce. Keep predictions to one whispered word.

study.overview: A butterfly grows and changes in four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult butterfly. The stages always come in the same order. A caterpillar and an adult butterfly look very different. When the adult lays new eggs, the stages start again and go around like a circle, just like the bean plant.

points.heading: Four stages in a set order
points.explanation: A butterfly’s life cycle has four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult butterfly. The order never changes. Example: a monarch butterfly lays a tiny round egg on a milkweed leaf. That is the first stage. To help you remember, say the stages with the class gestures: a tiny dot with your finger and thumb, a wiggling finger, arms wrapped tight, then flapping arms. You can also touch one finger for each stage as you say its name.

points.heading: What happens at each stage
points.explanation: A tiny caterpillar hatches from the egg. It eats leaves and grows bigger. Then it forms a chrysalis, which hangs still on a twig or leaf. Inside, the animal changes. At the end, an adult butterfly comes out with wings. Example: a monarch caterpillar munches milkweed leaves day after day, and its body gets much bigger. In The Very Hungry Caterpillar, Eric Carle uses the word cocoon. A butterfly caterpillar really makes a chrysalis. Many moth caterpillars are the ones that spin a cocoon.

points.heading: A caterpillar and a butterfly look different
points.explanation: A caterpillar has a long, soft body, many legs and no wings. It crawls and eats leaves. An adult butterfly has four wings and six legs. It flies and sips nectar, a sweet juice from flowers. Example: picture a green caterpillar slowly crawling along a leaf. Then picture a colorful butterfly flying from flower to flower. They are the same kind of animal at two different stages, but they do not look alike. When you compare them, look at the wings, the body and what each one does.

points.heading: The cycle goes around
points.explanation: The adult butterfly lays new eggs. Each egg is the start of a new life cycle, so the stages go around like a circle. The bean plant goes around in a circle too. Example: the monarch that came out of a chrysalis lays eggs on milkweed leaves. Tiny caterpillars hatch from those eggs, and the circle begins again. When you draw the butterfly stages, put them in a circle with arrows to show that they keep going.

study.overview: Last time you learned the four stages of a butterfly. In this lesson you put picture cards in order and told what happens at each stage. You learned what a caterpillar does while it grows. You also drew your bean again to see how it changed. This guide will help you remember the main ideas.

points.heading: The four stages go in a set order
points.explanation: A butterfly changes in four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult butterfly. The stages always come in this order. You can say the order with the words first, next, then and last. Each stage has a picture. The egg is tiny and round and sits on a milkweed leaf. The chrysalis is a green case that hangs still from a twig. The adult has open orange and black wings. The adult butterfly lays new eggs, so the life cycle makes a circle. Try this at home: hold up one finger for each word as you say first, next, then, last and name a stage with each one.

points.heading: The caterpillar eats and grows
points.explanation: The caterpillar’s job is to eat leaves and grow. A monarch caterpillar eats milkweed leaves almost all the time. Picture three photos of one caterpillar on one leaf. In the first it is tiny. In the second it is middle-sized. In the third it is big, and the leaf is mostly eaten. Eating leaves is how it got bigger. A caterpillar has no wings and does not fly. The growing happens in the caterpillar stage. The chrysalis is where the body changes. Say “eat, grow” and make a munching motion with your hands.

points.heading: Molting: a caterpillar sheds its skin
points.explanation: As a caterpillar grows, its outer skin gets too tight. New skin forms underneath. Then the caterpillar sheds the old skin. This is called molting. It is a bit like a shirt that gets too tight, except the caterpillar already has a new skin under the old one. After molting, the caterpillar keeps eating and keeps growing. Remember the three words: eat, grow, molt.

points.heading: Scientists compare now with before
points.explanation: Your bean journal is a record. Each time you draw, you look back at your last drawing first. Then you draw the bean as it looks today. Then you finish two sentences: “Today my bean has ___” and “Since last time, my bean ___.” Suppose a student named Sam drew only a root last time. If Sam sees a root and a stem today, Sam can write that the bean grew a stem. A bean that has not changed much is still a good record. Scientists write down what they really see. Keep the bag sealed. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. Wash your hands afterward.

study.overview: A frog has a life cycle with four stages in a set order. The stages go around like a circle, just like the bean plant and the butterfly. In this guide you can read again how a frog grows and how a tadpole changes as it gets legs.

points.heading: Four stages in a set order
points.explanation: A frog grows through four stages: egg → tadpole → froglet → adult frog. They always come in this order. A frog egg is laid in water, in a clump, and each egg is covered in clear jelly. A tadpole hatches from the egg. It has a tail, it swims, and it lives in water. A froglet is a young frog with four legs and a short stub of tail. An adult frog lives mostly on land near water. A tadpole is not a fish. It is a young frog. Example: you can show the stages with your hands. Wobble cupped hands for the jelly egg. Wiggle one hand for the tadpole’s tail. Make small hops with your fingers for the froglet. Make one big hop for the adult frog.

points.heading: How a tadpole changes as it grows
points.explanation: A tadpole changes slowly, over many weeks. Back legs grow first. Then front legs grow. While this happens, the tail gets shorter. The tail does not fall off. The body uses it up as the tadpole grows. A tadpole also grows lungs. Lungs help it breathe air, so it can leave the water as a froglet. In the water, a tadpole breathes with gills. Example: look at a tadpole with two small back legs and a long tail. When it grows more, you will see four legs and a shorter tail. You can say it with the sentence frames: “First the tadpole has a long tail and no legs. Next it grows back legs. Last it grows front legs and its tail gets shorter.”

points.heading: The cycle goes around like a circle
points.explanation: The adult frog lays new eggs in water. Then the stages start again, so they go around like a circle. Draw the four stages in a circle and add arrows between them. The bean plant goes around too: seed → sprout → seedling → grown plant with flowers → pods holding new seeds, then back to seed. The butterfly goes around: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → adult butterfly, then back to egg. Here is one way a frog and a butterfly are alike. Both start as eggs. Both change a lot as they grow. The young one does not look like the adult. A caterpillar does not look like a butterfly, and a tadpole does not look like an adult frog.

study.overview: A frog changes a lot as it grows. It does not look the same at every stage. Frogs also live in different places as they grow up. In this guide you will read about the order of the frog stages, where each stage lives, and how frogs make a circle. You will also read how scientists, like you, check how the bean has grown.

points.heading: Four stages in a set order
points.explanation: A frog’s life has four stages: egg, tadpole, froglet and adult frog. They always come in the same order. Use the words first, next, then and last to tell the order. Try the hand moves we used in class. Wobble your hands for the egg. Wiggle one hand like a tail for the tadpole. Do small hops for the froglet. Do one big hop for the adult frog. Do the moves in order and say each stage as you go. Do not skip the froglet. It is the stage between the tadpole and the adult.

points.heading: Water stages and land stages
points.explanation: The egg and the tadpole live in water. The tadpole breathes with gills, like a fish. The froglet and the adult frog live on land near water. They breathe air with lungs. Here is a clue for a froglet. A froglet still has a short tail, but it also has four legs and lungs. So it can climb out of the water. Suppose you see a small frog with four legs and a short tail sitting on a rock at the edge of a pond. You can tell it is a froglet. It is just leaving the water.

points.heading: The life cycle goes around like a circle
points.explanation: When a frog is grown, its life cycle is not over. The adult frog goes back to the water. There it lays new eggs in clear jelly. Then the new eggs start the stages again. This is why we call it a cycle. Put your finger on the adult frog card and trace an arrow back to the egg card. Your finger makes a circle. The circle shows that the stages keep going around.

points.heading: Comparing to see how the bean grew
points.explanation: Scientists look at what they see now and compare it with what they saw before. That is why you look back at your last journal drawing before you draw the bean again. Suppose your last drawing showed a short root. Today you might see a longer root and a stem. That change tells you the bean has grown. Label the parts you know, like root, stem or leaf. Some beans grow slowly. That is fine, because it is still a true record. Keep the bean bag sealed. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. Wash your hands after you touch the bags.

slides.title: What is the same?

slides.title: Three life cycles side by side
bullets: compare: look at two things to see how they are alike and how they are different
slides.notes: Before this slide appears, draw three circles on the board in a row: bean, butterfly and frog. Each student tells a partner the stages of one life cycle in order. Partners take turns, then switch to a different life cycle. Listen for a skipped chrysalis or froglet. Accept any wording that can be understood. Now show the slide and fill in each circle with the class. Expect students to notice that the bean has five stages and the butterfly and frog have four. Point out that every circle has an arrow from the last stage back to the first. Then say the word compare and read its meaning aloud. Read the stage names aloud for any student who needs it.

bullets: Bean cards: top row
Butterfly cards: middle row
Frog cards: bottom row
In each row, the first stage goes on the left
Pick two cards that look very different. Tell a partner why.
slides.notes: Hand out the envelopes of bean, butterfly and frog stage cards, mixed up, with a sorting mat for each pair. Pairs lay the bean cards in a row, then the butterfly cards under it, then the frog cards under that, each first to last. Each row starts on the left. Give about four minutes for the rows and three for the questions. Then pairs pick up two cards that look very different and tell a partner why. Expected pairs: caterpillar and adult butterfly; tadpole and adult frog. Note that the cycles begin with a seed, an egg and an egg. If a card is misplaced, ask which stage comes before it. slides.title: How are they alike? How are they different?
bullets: The ___ and the ___ are alike. Both ___.
The ___ and the ___ are different. The ___ has ___, but the ___ has ___.
slides.notes: Read both frames aloud. Partners take turns telling each other one way two life cycles are alike, using the first frame and pointing to the cards. Then they take turns again with one way two life cycles are different, using the second frame. Keep each turn to one short sentence. Hear one idea for alike and one for different, and write each on the board under Alike or Different. Ideas to listen for. Alike: start small as a seed or an egg; grow and change; go around like a circle. Different: the bean has five stages, the others four; the caterpillar and tadpole look unlike their adults; the bean stays in one place. Accept any wording that can be understood.

slides.title: Which sentence is true?
bullets: A: In every life cycle, the young one looks just like the adult.
B: In some life cycles, the young one looks very different from the adult.
slides.notes: Read both statements aloud. Each student chooses A or B, then writes or draws a reason on a whiteboard. They may use the cards on the mat. Partners compare answers and help each other say the reason. Hear two or three, then agree on one class answer. Keep the answer to yourself until students have given their reasons. The answer is B. A caterpillar has no wings and many legs, a butterfly has four wings and six legs. A tadpole has a tail and no legs, a frog has four legs. If students pick A, ask them to hold up the caterpillar card and the butterfly card. Praise reasons that name legs, wings or a tail. Then ask: in which life cycle does a young one look like the adult? The bean: a seedling looks like a small bean plant.

slides.title: Tell it on your whiteboard
bullets: Pick two life cycles. Write or draw one way they are alike and one way they are different.
slides.notes: Read the prompt aloud. Each student picks two life cycles and writes or draws one way they are alike and one way they are different. A few words or a quick drawing is enough for each idea. Spelling does not matter if the word can be read. Partners swap boards and read each other’s ideas. Hear one student. Ideas you may see. Alike: both go around like a circle, both start as eggs, both grow and change. Different: the bean cycle has five stages, but the butterfly cycle has four; the butterfly cycle has a chrysalis, but the frog cycle has a tadpole. Check-in only.

study.overview:
Today you compared three life cycles: the bean plant, the butterfly and the frog. To compare means to look at two things and tell how they are alike and how they are different. You found that all three cycles have things in common. You also found that some stages look very different from the adult. Here are the three life cycles, in order:

Bean: seed → sprout → seedling → grown plant with flowers → pods with new seeds

Butterfly: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → adult butterfly

Frog: egg → tadpole → froglet → adult frog

points.heading: To compare is to tell how things are alike and different
points.explanation: When you compare, you look at two things and say one way they are the same and one way they are not. Use these sentence frames to help you. “The ___ and the ___ are alike. Both ___.” “The ___ and the ___ are different. The ___ has ___, but the ___ has ___.” Example: The bean and the butterfly are alike. Both grow and change. The bean and the butterfly are different. The bean has five stages, but the butterfly has four.

points.heading: What all three life cycles share
points.explanation: Each life cycle has stages in a set order. The stages always go in the same order, and you cannot skip one. Each cycle also begins small, as a seed or as an egg. Each cycle goes around like a circle, too. The last stage leads back to the first. Example: the last bean stage is pods with new seeds. Those seeds can be planted, and then a new bean cycle begins.

points.heading: Some stages look very different
points.explanation: In some life cycles, the young one does not look like the adult. A caterpillar has no wings and many legs. An adult butterfly has four wings and six legs. A tadpole has a tail and no legs. An adult frog has four legs. When you explain a difference, name the body parts you can see, like legs, wings or a tail. That makes your reason strong.

points.heading: Not every young one looks different
points.explanation: Some young living things look like a small copy of the adult. A bean seedling looks like a small bean plant. It has a stem and leaves, just like the grown plant. So it is not true that every young living thing looks different from its adult. Remember this when you compare. Ask yourself what the young one looks like and what the adult looks like. Then tell how they match or do not match.

blocks.text: Lay your cards on the mat. Put the bean cards in the top row, the butterfly cards in the middle row and the frog cards in the bottom row. In each row, put the first stage on the left and go in order to the right.

study.overview: Every living thing does four things in its life cycle: it is born, it grows, it reproduces and it dies. Your bean did these things, and so does a dog, a tree and a chicken. The stages can look very different, but the four things stay the same. In this guide you will read what each word means and why a life cycle goes around like a circle. You will also read how to draw and label a life cycle. Next time you will draw and label the stages of one life cycle on your own. This is the Life cycle drawing and labeling assessment, and it is 100% of the unit grade. It is scored with a simple rubric with four levels: Excellent, Good, Developing and Beginning.

points.heading: The four things every living thing does
points.explanation: Born means a new living thing starts its life. Grow means it gets bigger and changes. Reproduce means it makes new living things of the same kind. Die means its life ends. Think about a bean plant. It is born as a tiny plant inside a seed. It grows into a sprout, a seedling and a bigger plant. It makes pods that hold new seeds. Later the old plant dries up and turns brown. A rock does not do all four things, so a rock is not a living thing.

points.heading: What reproduce means
points.explanation: To reproduce means to make new living things of the same kind. A bean plant makes seeds in pods, and each seed can grow into a new bean plant. A dog can have puppies, and puppies grow up to be dogs. A tree makes new seeds that can grow into new trees. A butterfly and a frog lay eggs. The new living things are always the same kind as their parents. Bean seeds never grow into dogs.

points.heading: Why a life cycle goes around like a circle
points.explanation: Living things reproduce, so the end of one life cycle is the start of the next one. Look at the bean. The new seeds in the pods are the start of new bean plants. The cycle comes back to where it began, so we draw it as a circle. The bean, the butterfly and the frog all do the same four things. Their stages look different, but all of them go around.

points.heading: How to draw and label a life cycle
points.explanation: Use four steps. First, draw each stage in its own box. Second, put the boxes in order. Third, add arrows all the way around the circle, including one from the last stage back to the first. Fourth, write a label under each box. A label is just the name of the stage. Here is an example with a chicken: egg, chick, young chicken, adult hen. Draw four boxes in a circle with a picture in each. Put an arrow from each box to the next. Then write egg, chick, young chicken and adult hen under the boxes. Before you finish, check four things. Are the stages in order? Is there a picture in each box? Is there a label under each? Do the arrows go all the way around? When you draw your own life cycle, use your stage cards and your journal to see how each stage looks.

handouts.key:
My name: The student’s name.
The life cycle I picked: Bean, butterfly or frog; the choice matches the drawing.
What to do: Look for one of these sequences, with a recognizable picture in each box and a readable stage label under it:
Bean: seed → sprout → seedling → grown plant → pods with new seeds → seed.
Butterfly: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → adult butterfly → egg.
Frog: egg → tadpole → froglet → adult frog → egg.
Accept matching stage names such as adult bean plant for grown plant. Accept readable spelling such as krisalis. Arrows connect every box in order and return to the starting stage. The return arrow represents a new generation. Common slips include missing the return arrow, reversing arrows, leaving a stage unlabeled or putting stages out of order.
If you finish early: Accept any correctly placed word or words. For bean, born fits the seed containing the tiny plant; grow fits sprout, seedling or grown plant; reproduce fits pods with new seeds. For butterfly, born fits hatching from the egg; grow fits the caterpillar; reproduce fits the adult laying eggs. For frog, born fits hatching from the egg; grow fits the tadpole or froglet; reproduce fits the adult laying eggs. Die means an individual’s life ends. Accept it beside a separate drawing or note showing death; it is not a required stage between the adult and its offspring.

points.heading: What a life cycle drawing needs
points.explanation: Check four things. First, the stages are in order, the way the living thing really grows and changes. Second, every box has a picture. Third, every picture has a label under it that names the stage. Fourth, the arrows go from each stage to the next and all the way around. Here is a chicken example. A good chicken drawing has four boxes: an egg, a small fluffy chick, a young chicken with some feathers and a full-grown hen. Each box has a picture and a label, and the arrows go in a circle. Use these four checks on your own drawing before you stop.

points.heading: The last arrow makes a cycle
points.explanation: The arrow from the last stage back to the first stage shows that living things reproduce. The grown-up makes new living things, and the life cycle starts again. That is why the drawing goes around like a circle and does not stop at a line. In a chicken drawing, the arrow goes from the full-grown hen back to the egg, because the hen lays eggs and new chicks hatch. This also helps you remember what all living things do. They are born, they grow, they reproduce and they die.

points.heading: How the drawing is scored
points.explanation: Your drawing is scored by counting problems. Each stage can have at most one stage problem: the stage is left out, it has no picture, or its label is missing or wrong. Order is counted separately. Count one problem for each stage that must move to put the order right. Use the fewest moves among the stages shown. If the arrows do not go all the way around, count one more problem. Then find your level: 0 problems is Excellent, 1 is Good, 2 is Developing, and 3 or more is Beginning. Here is a worked example, Drawing B. It shows a chicken life cycle with four boxes. The pictures are an egg, a small fluffy chick, a full-grown hen and a half-grown young chicken. The labels match the pictures: egg, chick, adult hen, young chicken. The arrows go from egg to chick, chick to adult hen, and adult hen to young chicken. No arrow goes back to the egg. The pictures and labels match, so there is no stage problem. The adult hen and the young chicken are swapped. Moving one stage, the adult hen to the end, fixes the order, so that is one problem. The missing arrow back to the egg is one more problem. Two problems is Developing.

points.heading: Check your own work
points.explanation: Before you finish, read your drawing the way a scorer would. Point to each box and ask: Is this stage in the right place? Is there a picture? Is there a label under it? Then follow the arrows with your finger, all the way from the last stage back to the first. Fix a missing arrow or a missing label right away. Spelling does not count toward your score. A label that can be read, such as “krisalis”, is accepted. Your drawing is your own work, so use what you have learned and your own careful looking.

t_4b50f2532a22.prompt: Which thing belongs in the living group?

t_5de54a48a25f.prompt: A rose bush is living, even though it stays in one place.

t_73ccb82eb88e.prompt: Maya says a balloon is living because it moves through the air. What would you tell Maya? Give one reason.

t_4d70504e417d.explanation: The bean cycle begins with a seed, and the frog cycle begins with an egg. “A bean begins as an egg; a frog begins as a seed” switches the starting stages. “A bean has a tadpole; a frog has a seedling” switches stages from the two cycles. “A bean has a chrysalis; a frog has a sprout” mixes up butterfly and bean stages with the frog cycle.

t_d2863bf535a2.prompt: A froglet comes before a tadpole in the frog life cycle, just as a sprout comes before a seedling in the bean life cycle.
t_d2863bf535a2.explanation: A sprout comes before a seedling, but a tadpole comes before a froglet.

t_db8a8611f53e.prompt: A student says, “Only the butterfly life cycle goes around like a circle.” Which answer explains the mistake?

choices.text: The bean and frog life cycles stop when they become adults.
The bean and frog life cycles also go around like a circle.
The bean and frog life cycles go backward through their stages.
The bean and frog life cycles have no stages in order.

t_db8a8611f53e.explanation: All three life cycles go around like a circle. “The bean and frog life cycles stop when they become adults” leaves out the next generation. “The bean and frog life cycles go backward through their stages” gives the wrong direction. “The bean and frog life cycles have no stages in order” misses that each cycle has a set order.

t_f4c06c7fed66.prompt: Compare the bean and butterfly life cycles. Tell one way they are different.
t_f4c06c7fed66.answer: A bean plant has a seedling stage, but a butterfly has a caterpillar stage.
t_f4c06c7fed66.explanation: A seedling is a stage in the bean life cycle. A caterpillar is a stage in the butterfly life cycle. Other accurate differences are also acceptable.

t_1f0581753d6e.prompt: A sunflower gets taller and grows new leaves. Which life cycle word fits this change?
t_1f0581753d6e.explanation: Grow means a living thing gets bigger and changes. Born means its life starts; reproduce means it makes new living things of the same kind; die means its life ends.

t_4567d1f4e260.prompt: An adult ladybug lays eggs. Which life cycle word describes what the ladybug is doing?
t_4567d1f4e260.explanation: Reproducing means making new living things of the same kind. Being born means starting life; growing means getting bigger and changing; dying means life ends.

t_0485a3223439.prompt: A goldfish grows and can reproduce during its life cycle.
t_0485a3223439.explanation: A goldfish grows and changes. Adult goldfish can reproduce, making new goldfish.

t_939c96ae5e57.prompt: Maya draws a butterfly life cycle: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → adult butterfly. What should she add to show the cycle goes around?

choices.text: An arrow from the egg to the chrysalis
An arrow from the caterpillar to the egg
An arrow from the chrysalis to the caterpillar
An arrow from the adult butterfly to the egg

t_939c96ae5e57.explanation: An arrow from the adult butterfly to the egg shows that an adult can lay eggs and the cycle can begin again. An arrow from the egg to the chrysalis skips the caterpillar; an arrow from the caterpillar to the egg points backward; an arrow from the chrysalis to the caterpillar also points backward.

t_9d9bf0153a31.prompt: A student draws a frog life cycle in this order: egg → froglet → tadpole → adult frog. What is the mistake? Write the stages in the correct order and explain where the last arrow should go.
t_9d9bf0153a31.answer: The tadpole and froglet are in the wrong order. The correct order is egg → tadpole → froglet → adult frog. The last arrow goes from the adult frog back to the egg.
t_9d9bf0153a31.explanation: A tadpole changes into a froglet, and a froglet grows into an adult frog. The arrow back to the egg shows that adult frogs can lay eggs.

t_9f5858fb0b8a.prompt: A drawing shows the frog stages in this order: egg, tadpole, adult frog, froglet. How can you fix the order by moving one stage?

Move the tadpole after the froglet.

Move the adult frog after the froglet.

t_9f5858fb0b8a.explanation: The froglet comes before the adult frog. Moving the adult frog after the froglet puts the stages in order. Moving the egg after the tadpole puts the egg too late. t_8906b1b35799.prompt: A butterfly drawing shows an egg, a caterpillar, a chrysalis and an adult butterfly in order. Which arrows complete the cycle?

Egg → chrysalis → caterpillar → adult butterfly → egg

t_e9a311e590f9.prompt: A picture of a froglet in a frog life cycle should be labeled tadpole.
t_e9a311e590f9.explanation: A picture of a froglet should be labeled froglet. A tadpole is an earlier stage.

t_a9eee1759131.prompt: A bean life cycle drawing shows a young plant with a stem and its first leaves. Which label names that stage?
t_a9eee1759131.explanation: A seedling is a young plant with a stem and leaves. A bean seed is the stage before the sprout. A new sprout is an earlier stage as the seed begins to grow. A bean pod appears later on the grown plant.

t_71e0db1749e3.prompt: A butterfly drawing has four boxes in this order: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult butterfly. Each box has a matching picture and label. t_71e0db1749e3.answer: Add an arrow from the adult butterfly back to the egg. It shows that the adult reproduces and the cycle goes around again.
t_71e0db1749e3.explanation: The stages and labels are in order, but the arrows do not return to the beginning. The arrow from the adult butterfly to the egg shows reproduction and completes the cycle.

t_940adf566b58.title: Life cycle drawing and labeling assessment
t_940adf566b58.prompt: Draw and label one life cycle: a bean, a butterfly or a frog. Work on your own. This assessment is 100% of the unit grade. It is due at the start of the next school day.
steps: Choose the bean, the butterfly or the frog. Draw each stage in its own box, in order.
Write the name of each stage under its box. Add arrows from each stage to the next and from the last stage back to the first. Check your drawing.
t_940adf566b58.answerKey:
1. A strong drawing shows one complete cycle, with a picture in each box. Bean: seed, sprout, seedling, grown plant with flowers, pods. Butterfly: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult butterfly. Frog: egg, tadpole, froglet, adult frog. Usual mistakes include leaving out a stage, leaving a box without a picture, or placing stages out of order.
2. A strong drawing has a matching label under every box and arrows connecting the stages all the way around, including from the last stage back to the first. Count at most one stage problem for each stage that is missing, has no picture, or has a missing or wrong label. Separately, count one order problem for each stage that must move to fix the order, using the fewest moves among stages shown. Count one problem if the arrows do not go all the way around. A stage can have both a stage problem and an order problem. Accept readable spelling such as “krisalis.”

f_0fa2bcf30d69.question: If something moves, is it alive?
f_0fa2bcf30d69.answer: No. Moving is not the test for life. A toy car moves when you push it, but it does not eat, grow or have baby cars, so it is not alive. An oak tree stays in one place, but it needs water, it grows and it makes seeds, so it is alive.

f_e53c78b9fcff.question: A dry bean seed does not move. How can it be alive?
f_e53c78b9fcff.answer: A dry bean seed holds a tiny living plant inside. It is resting until it gets water. That is why we put our seeds in damp paper towels. Planting them will show us what happens.

f_bf291b5d11d7.question: Why can’t we see the beans change in the bags today?
f_bf291b5d11d7.answer: Seeds change slowly. Roots usually show in about three to seven days, so nothing will look different today. Next time we will look in the bags for the first changes. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. We wash our hands after we touch them.

f_a905dd12db59.question: Is the baby plant inside the bean really alive?
f_a905dd12db59.answer: Yes. Given water, it grows the root you will see in your bag, then leaves. It is tiny and pale, about the size of a grain of rice. Before you peel the seed, find the small mark: the baby plant lies just under that spot. Use your hand lens to find it. It rests between the two food halves, and the food feeds it until it can make its own.

f_806f30934ff3.question: My bean in the bag looks the same as before. Did I do something wrong?
f_806f30934ff3.answer: No. Seeds change slowly. After about a day a seed may look bigger, or its seed coat may start to split. Roots usually show in about three to seven days. If you see no change, write that it looks the same. That is a real observation. We keep the bag closed and look through it with a hand lens.

f_58ec33877e57.question: Can I taste the bean?
f_58ec33877e57.answer: No. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. Keep seeds and seed pieces out of your mouth, nose and ears. Wash your hands when you finish, and put the pieces on the tray so we can throw them in the trash.

f_88b967a34d17.question: My bean in the bag does not have a root yet. Did I do something wrong?
f_88b967a34d17.answer: No. Seeds grow at different speeds, and some bags show a root before others do. Draw exactly what you see. A seed with no root yet matches the seed card, and you can say it is not a sprout yet.

f_6b3d99c2ce10.question: Why do the bean stages go around like a circle?
f_6b3d99c2ce10.answer: The pods hold new seeds. Each new seed can grow into a new bean plant, and that plant makes pods with more seeds. So the stages keep going around, and we can start our picture at the seed.

f_587be407e732.question: Why can’t we open the bag or eat the beans?
f_587be407e732.answer: The bags stay sealed, and beans are for looking at, never for eating. We look through the bag with a hand lens and draw what we see. Then everyone washes their hands.

f_4e6e7d1ff964.question: Why does the caterpillar eat so much?
f_4e6e7d1ff964.answer: A caterpillar eats leaves to get the food its body needs to grow. It starts out tiny and gets much bigger before it changes. That is why the caterpillar in the book keeps eating and eating.

f_f49c0cbb109c.question: The book says cocoon. Is that the right word?
f_f49c0cbb109c.answer: The book uses the word cocoon. A butterfly caterpillar makes a chrysalis, and that is the word we use in science class. Many moth caterpillars wrap themselves in a cocoon, so the two words are easy to mix up.

f_e0ae43b4d82c.question: Does a butterfly eat leaves like a caterpillar does?
f_e0ae43b4d82c.answer: No. An adult butterfly sips nectar, a sweet juice from flowers. A caterpillar crawls and chews leaves. Their bodies are different, so they eat in different ways.

f_ff3f9de1153b.question: Why does my bean look almost the same as last time?
f_ff3f9de1153b.answer: Seeds grow at different speeds. Draw exactly what you see today. Then look back at your last drawing and compare. You can write that your bean has not changed much yet. A slow bean is still a good record, because scientists compare what they see now with what they saw before.

f_c7f6dcc3662b.question: Why do we say “first, next, then, last” when we put the cards in a row?
f_c7f6dcc3662b.answer: Those words tell us the order things happen in. A butterfly’s stages always come in the same set order, so each card has its own place on the mat. When you trace your finger from the adult back to the egg, you see a circle. That is because the adult butterfly lays new eggs, and the life cycle starts again.

f_d79dd5477e42.question: Can I open the bag to touch my bean, or taste it?
f_d79dd5477e42.answer: No. The bag stays sealed so the bean can keep growing, and the bean is only for looking at. Use your hand lens to look through the bag. Then put the bag back in the sunny window and wash your hands.

f_1880d38f04e1.question: How do I spell chrysalis in my journal?
f_1880d38f04e1.answer: It sounds like KRIS-uh-lis. Write it the way it sounds, and sound it out slowly. Spelling does not matter in your journal as long as the word can be read. You can also copy it from your card.

f_53c9030171e8.question: Is a tadpole a fish?
f_53c9030171e8.answer: No. A tadpole is a young frog. It lives in water and swims with its tail, so it looks a little like a fish. But it will grow legs and become a frog.

f_d29931fdd807.question: Does the tadpole’s tail fall off?
f_d29931fdd807.answer: No. The tail gets shorter little by little. The tadpole’s body uses it up as the tadpole grows.

f_3e6ce8a1c0cd.question: How can a froglet leave the water if a tadpole lives in water?
f_3e6ce8a1c0cd.answer: A tadpole breathes with gills, which work in water. As it grows, it develops lungs. Lungs help it breathe air, so it can leave the water as a froglet.

f_cab53cc576a9.question: Why do we say a frog’s life goes in a circle?
f_cab53cc576a9.answer: The adult frog lays new eggs in water. Those eggs start the stages again. The bean plant and the butterfly go around like a circle too.

f_f3d0a5e8dcf6.question: Why does my bean look different from my partner’s bean?
f_f3d0a5e8dcf6.answer: Beans grow at their own speed. Some have longer roots or a leaf already, and some are slower. Draw what your bean looks like today. Then look at your last drawing and say how your bean changed.

f_f53cc2fb5548.question: How can a tadpole breathe in the water?
f_f53cc2fb5548.answer: A tadpole breathes with gills. Gills take in air that is mixed into the water. A froglet grows lungs, and lungs breathe air.

f_bcb9eb0b93d4.question: Why do we keep the bean bags sealed? Can I eat a bean?
f_bcb9eb0b93d4.answer: No. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. The bags stay closed so the beans stay clean and keep growing. Look through the bag with your hand lens, and wash your hands after you touch the bags and cards.

f_471ac48731c7.question: What if I do not know how to spell a word in my journal?
f_471ac48731c7.answer: Write it the way it sounds. If someone can read your word, it is fine. You can also draw the part and write the label as well as you can.

f_cce3315e3022.question: Why does a caterpillar look so different from a butterfly?
f_cce3315e3022.answer: They are the same animal at two different stages. A caterpillar has no wings and many legs. An adult butterfly has four wings and six legs. The animal changes a lot as it grows, and the chrysalis stage comes in between.

f_eded3454c3f9.question: Does every young living thing look different from its adult?
f_eded3454c3f9.answer: No. A tadpole does not look like an adult frog, but a bean seedling looks like a small bean plant. Some young living things change a lot and some change less.

f_6eb0299c4f42.question: Can I eat the beans or taste them?
f_6eb0299c4f42.answer: No. Beans are for looking at, never for eating. The sprouting bags stay sealed, and we wash our hands after we touch the bags or the cards.

f_37610c2e808d.question: What does reproduce mean?
f_37610c2e808d.answer: To reproduce means to make new living things of the same kind. A bean plant makes seeds in pods, and each seed can grow into a new bean plant. A butterfly and a frog lay eggs, and the eggs hatch into new butterflies and frogs.

f_4143477c2120.question: Why does a life cycle go around like a circle?
f_4143477c2120.answer: Living things reproduce, so a new life starts and the cycle begins again. Think about a bean plant. It makes pods with new seeds, and those seeds can grow into new bean plants. That is why we draw arrows all the way around and do not stop at the last stage.

f_9424d0ed95a9.question: Why is die one of the four things?
f_9424d0ed95a9.answer: Every living thing’s life ends one day. This is a normal part of every life cycle. An old bean plant dries up and turns brown after it makes its pods. Before that happens, living things reproduce, so new living things of the same kind keep starting their lives.

f_1bcfbaf3e488.question: Do I have to spell every label perfectly?
f_1bcfbaf3e488.answer: No. Spelling does not count toward your score. If your label can be read, it is correct. A label like “krisalis” is fine. What matters is that each label names the right stage. If you want the prompt read aloud to you, just ask.

f_7524aee07264.question: Why does the last stage need an arrow back to the first one?
f_7524aee07264.answer: Living things reproduce, and that starts the cycle again. The arrow from the last stage back to the first shows this, so the cycle goes around like a circle. Your arrows should go all the way around with no gap.

f_233572624202.question: Which life cycle can I draw, and what if I don’t finish?
f_233572624202.answer: You may pick the bean, the butterfly or the frog. The bean has five stages. The butterfly and the frog each have four. Draw every stage in its own box, in order, with a picture and a label. If you are not finished when time is up, keep working on your own. The Life cycle drawing and labeling assessment is due at the start of the next school day.
